title: How Voltaire beat the lottery with its cheapest tickets
description:
In 1729 France ran a lottery to sell its bonds: only bondholders could play, a ticket cost a thousandth of the bond's value, and every ticket had the same chance at a 500,000-livre jackpot. So a 100,000-livre bond paid 100 livres for one ticket, while 100 small 1,000-livre bonds got 100 tickets for the same 100 livres: 100 times the chance. Charles de La Condamine spotted it, Voltaire and 11 others pooled money to buy up small bonds, and the group won month after month until the lottery was shut down; Voltaire's share was about half a million livres.

Numbers checked in code: the ticket prices exactly and 200,000 simulated draws. Sources: Smithsonian Magazine, Voltaire, Enlightenment Philosopher and Lottery Scammer; Damn Interesting, The Enlightenment Guide to Winning the Lottery; Wikipedia, Charles Marie de La Condamine.

beats.say: Voltaire beat the lottery with its cheapest tickets.
No luck, no cheating. He read the rules better than the government.
Paris, 1729. France runs a lottery to sell its bonds.
Rule one: a ticket costs a thousandth of your bond. A 100,000 livre bond pays 100. A 1,000 livre bond pays one.
Rule two: every ticket has the same chance at the jackpot. 500,000 livres.
Spot the flaw? The price grows with the bond. The chance doesn't.
So buy small bonds. The 100 livres a rich player pays for one ticket buys you 100. 100 times the chance.
Now team up and buy the small bonds. La Condamine, Voltaire and 11 friends did.
They won month after month. Voltaire made about half a million livres. Then the lottery was shut down.
